case: State of Israel v. Benjamin Netanyahu et al.: Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000 (bribery, fraud and breach of trust)
description: Police investigations opened from late 2016 led Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit to announce on 21 November 2019 an indictment of Netanyahu, then prime minister, on three counts of fraud and breach of trust and one count of bribery. In Case 1000 prosecutors allege that he received luxury gifts (cigars, champagne and jewellery for his wife) worth hundreds of thousands of shekels from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian businessman James Packer while acting on matters of interest to Milchan. In Case 2000 he is alleged to have discussed with Yedioth Ahronoth publisher Arnon Mozes more favourable coverage in exchange for legislation curbing the rival free daily Israel Hayom. In Case 4000, the only one with a bribery count, he is alleged to have approved, as communications minister, regulatory decisions worth hundreds of millions of shekels to Bezeq's controlling shareholder Shaul Elovitch in return for favourable coverage on Elovitch's Walla news site. Netanyahu requested parliamentary immunity on 1 January 2020 and withdrew the request on 28 January 2020, when the indictment was filed with the Jerusalem District Court. He denies all wrongdoing and calls the cases a politically motivated ‘witch hunt’ and an attempted ‘coup’; on finishing his testimony he said the investigation had been ‘a political assassination’ that ‘found nothing’.
outcome: No verdict as of 22 October 2026. The trial opened on 24 May 2020 before judges Rivka Friedman-Feldman, Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham; the prosecution rested in July 2024. Netanyahu testified in 98 hearings between 10 December 2024 and 24 June 2026, partly in the Tel Aviv District Court for security reasons, with many sessions shortened or cancelled at his request for security and diplomatic reasons. The trial has since been in the defence-witness stage: former attorney general Mandelblit testified as a defence witness in October 2026, with further hearings scheduled. On 29 June 2026 the judges repeated their June 2023 suggestion that the prosecution drop the bribery count, which they consider difficult to prove; the prosecution had declined in 2023. Defence counsel Amit Hadad said the trial could not finish by March 2028 if the bribery count remained. A pardon request is pending separately (see related record).
court: Jerusalem District Court (hearings partly held at the Tel Aviv District Court)
presumption_note: Netanyahu is on trial and has not been convicted; he is presumed innocent and denies all the charges. No court has ruled on the merits as of October 2026. The judges' suggestion to drop the bribery count is a procedural recommendation, not a finding.
key_facts: 21 November 2019: attorney general announces the indictment; filed 28 January 2020 after Netanyahu withdrew his immunity request
24 May 2020: trial opens; first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial
July 2024: prosecution rests; Netanyahu's testimony runs from 10 December 2024 to 24 June 2026 (98 hearings)
29 June 2026: judges again recommend dropping the bribery charge in Case 4000
October 2026: defence witnesses, including former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit

case: Request for a presidential pardon in Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000
type: clemency proceeding before the President of Israel (Netanyahu as applicant)
description: On 30 November 2025 Netanyahu's lawyer Amit Hadad submitted a 111-page pardon request to President Isaac Herzog's legal department, with a letter signed by Netanyahu, asking for the trial to be ended. Netanyahu did not admit guilt, contested the charges and the process that led to them, and argued that ending the trial would ‘lower the flames and promote broad reconciliation’ and allow him to devote all his time to his duties. Herzog said he would weigh the ‘extraordinary request’ after expert opinions. US President Donald Trump repeatedly called on Herzog to pardon Netanyahu, including in a letter in November 2025 and in public remarks in February 2026; Herzog's office said Israel is ‘a sovereign state governed by the rule of law’. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said a pardon should require an admission of guilt, an expression of remorse and retirement from public life.
outcome: Undecided as of 22 October 2026. In March 2026 the Justice Ministry's Pardons Department said it could not determine that the pardon power applied to an ongoing trial without conviction or admission of guilt, and could not recommend it; Heritage Minister Amichay Eliyahu, acting for Justice Minister Yariv Levin, who recused himself, reportedly endorsed the request. On 26 April 2026 Herzog declined to decide for the time being and proposed mediating talks on a plea agreement between Netanyahu's lawyers and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara. The attorney general agreed to talks without preconditions; Netanyahu's team did not respond, and Channel 12 reported that he had decided not to join. Kan later reported that Herzog had frozen the initiative, which his office called incorrect. Netanyahu completed his testimony on 24 June 2026, which, the Times of Israel noted, could make moot the request's argument that spending days testifying in court keeps him from his duties.
court: President of the State of Israel (Pardons Department of the Ministry of Justice for the professional opinion)
presumption_note: A pardon request is not an admission of guilt; Netanyahu explicitly denies the charges and remains presumed innocent in the ongoing trial.
key_facts: 30 November 2025: formal pardon request submitted to President Herzog
March 2026: Pardons Department advises against granting it before conviction
26 April 2026: Herzog defers a decision and proposes mediation towards a plea deal
May 2026: attorney general agrees to talks; Netanyahu's legal team does not respond

case: International Criminal Court, Situation in the State of Palestine: arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu
type: international criminal proceeding (Netanyahu as suspect; arrest warrant issued)
description: On 20 May 2024 ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan applied for arrest warrants for Netanyahu and then defence minister Yoav Gallant, as well as Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Mohammed Deif. On 21 November 2024 Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously rejected Israel's challenges under Articles 18 and 19 of the Rome Statute (finding the jurisdiction challenge premature) and issued the warrants. It found reasonable grounds to believe that Netanyahu and Gallant bear criminal responsibility as co-perpetrators for the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution and other inhumane acts, and as civilian superiors for the war crime of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population of Gaza, for conduct from at least 8 October 2023 until at least 20 May 2024. Israel is not a party to the Rome Statute and rejects the court's jurisdiction, arguing that the Oslo Accords deny any Palestinian entity criminal jurisdiction over Israeli nationals. Netanyahu called it an ‘antisemitic decision’; his office said it rejected the accusations ‘with disgust’. The warrants for the three Hamas leaders were withdrawn after they were killed.
outcome: The warrant remains in force as of October 2026; Netanyahu has not been arrested. In April 2025 the Appeals Chamber ruled that the Pre-Trial Chamber had been wrong to dismiss Israel's jurisdiction challenge as premature and ordered it to examine it; on 16 July 2025 the Pre-Trial Chamber refused to withdraw the warrants while that challenge is pending, and on 17 October 2025 it refused Israel leave to appeal. On 15 December 2025 the Appeals Chamber rejected a further Israeli challenge concerning the scope of the investigation. No ruling on the remanded jurisdiction challenge was found in the sources consulted. The United States has imposed sanctions on ICC judges and the prosecutor in response to the warrants.
court: International Criminal Court (Pre-Trial Chamber I; Appeals Chamber), The Hague
presumption_note: An arrest warrant means only that judges found ‘reasonable grounds to believe’ the alleged crimes were committed; Netanyahu has not been charged at trial or convicted, is presumed innocent, and rejects the allegations and the court's jurisdiction.
key_facts: 20 May 2024: prosecutor applies for warrants
21 November 2024: warrants issued for Netanyahu and Gallant; Israel's challenges rejected
April 2025: Appeals Chamber orders the jurisdiction challenge to be re-examined
16 July and 17 October 2025: requests to withdraw the warrants and to appeal rejected
15 December 2025: Appeals Chamber rejects another Israeli appeal; warrants remain in place

case: Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office: arrest warrants for Netanyahu and 36 other Israeli officials (genocide and crimes against humanity)
type: foreign criminal investigation (Netanyahu as suspect; arrest warrant issued in absentia)
description: On 7 November 2025 the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office announced arrest warrants for 37 suspects, including Netanyahu, Defence Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, accusing them of ‘genocide and crimes against humanity’ that Israel had ‘perpetrated systematically’ in Gaza; the statement cited among other things the Israeli strike in March 2025 on the Turkish-built hospital in Gaza, which the Israeli army said Hamas was using. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said Israel ‘firmly rejects, with contempt’ the charges, calling them a ‘PR stunt’ by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Israel rejects genocide accusations as false and antisemitic. Turkey has also joined South Africa's case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
outcome: Warrants outstanding as of October 2026; Netanyahu does not travel to Turkey and no proceedings in his presence are possible. No further procedural step was reported in the sources consulted.
court: Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office (Republic of Türkiye)
presumption_note: The warrants are a prosecutor's accusation in a foreign jurisdiction that Israel does not recognise; Netanyahu has not been tried or convicted, is presumed innocent and Israel rejects the charges.
key_facts: 7 November 2025: warrants announced for 37 Israeli officials
Charges: genocide and crimes against humanity in Gaza
Israel rejects the warrants as a political stunt

case: State commission of inquiry into the submarine and naval vessels affair (Case 3000): warning to Netanyahu
type: state commission of inquiry (Netanyahu warned that he may be harmed by its findings; summoned to testify)
description: The state commission of inquiry headed by retired Supreme Court President Asher Grunis, established in 2022 under the Bennett government, examines Israel's purchases of submarines and naval vessels from the German shipbuilder Thyssenkrupp in the 2010s, deals worth about $2 billion, and Germany's sale of submarines and vessels to Egypt with Israel's apparent approval. In 2024 it issued warnings to Netanyahu, former defence minister Moshe Ya'alon, former Mossad director Yossi Cohen, former navy commander Ram Rothberg and former National Security Council official Avner Simchoni that they could be harmed by its findings. In January 2026 it published findings of ‘systemic failings’ in the acquisitions and said the sale of vessels to Egypt with Israel's approval endangered national security. The related criminal case led to indictments of several close confidants of Netanyahu, but not of Netanyahu himself. Netanyahu denies wrongdoing, including that he approved the 2014 German–Egyptian deal, and calls the probe a witch hunt.
outcome: On 21 October 2026 the commission summoned Netanyahu and the four other warned officials to give testimony behind closed doors, giving them an opportunity to defend themselves before any personal responsibility is attributed; hearings were reported to be planned for November–December 2026. No findings of personal responsibility have been issued.
court: State Commission of Inquiry into the Submarine Affair (chaired by Asher Grunis)
presumption_note: A state commission of inquiry is not a criminal court; a warning means only that its findings could affect Netanyahu. He has not been charged in connection with the affair and denies wrongdoing.
key_facts: 2022: commission established by the Bennett–Lapid government
2024: warning letters to Netanyahu and four others
January 2026: commission reports ‘systemic failings’
21 October 2026: Netanyahu summoned to testify under warning

case: State commission of inquiry into the 2021 Mount Meron disaster: finding of personal responsibility
type: state commission of inquiry (Netanyahu among the officials examined)
description: On 30 April 2021, during Lag BaOmer celebrations attended by about 100,000 people, mostly ultra-Orthodox, 45 men and boys were killed in a crush at the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on Mount Meron, Israel's deadliest civilian disaster. The state commission of inquiry, set up by the next government in June 2021, examined the conduct of officials, including Netanyahu, who was prime minister at the time.
outcome: In its final report of 6 March 2024 the commission, headed by retired judge Dvora Berliner, found that Netanyahu bore personal responsibility: there was ‘a reasonable basis to conclude’ that he knew the site had been improperly managed for years and posed a danger, and he ‘did not act as expected of a prime minister’ despite repeated warnings, including State Comptroller reports. Because of his position, it did not propose sanctions against him. It also named then public security minister Amir Ohana, police chief Kobi Shabtai and religious services minister Yaakov Avitan as personally responsible.
court: State Commission of Inquiry into the Mount Meron Disaster
presumption_note: The commission's finding of personal responsibility is an administrative finding, not a criminal charge or conviction; no proceedings against Netanyahu followed.
key_facts: 30 April 2021: 45 killed in the Meron crush
6 March 2024: final report finds Netanyahu personally responsible but proposes no sanction against him

case: Bar-On affair (1997): police recommendation to indict for fraud and breach of trust
type: criminal investigation (Netanyahu as suspect); no indictment
description: In January 1997 the cabinet approved lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney general; he stepped down two days later. A three-month police investigation followed an Israel Television report alleging that the appointment was part of a deal to secure a plea bargain for Shas leader Aryeh Deri, then on trial for corruption, in return for Shas's support for the Hebron agreement in cabinet. Police recommended indicting Netanyahu, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi, Prime Minister's Office director Avigdor Lieberman and Deri.
outcome: In April 1997 Attorney General Elyakim Rubinstein and State Prosecutor Edna Arbel decided there was insufficient evidence to indict Netanyahu and Hanegbi; only Deri was to be indicted. Petitions against the decision were heard by the High Court of Justice in 1997. No charges were brought against Netanyahu.
court: Israel Police; Attorney General of Israel; High Court of Justice (petitions)
presumption_note: Netanyahu was never charged; the prosecutors' decision cited insufficient evidence to bring charges. He is presumed innocent.
key_facts: January 1997: Bar-On appointed and resigns within two days
April 1997: no indictment of Netanyahu for lack of sufficient evidence

case: Amedi and state gifts affair (1999–2000): police recommendation to indict
type: criminal investigation (Netanyahu as suspect); no indictment
description: After Netanyahu left office in 1999, police investigated allegations that he had received about $100,000 in free services from a government contractor (the case became known as the Amedi affair) and that gifts presented to the state during his premiership had been kept by the family, and recommended that he be charged.
outcome: On 27 September 2000 Attorney General Elyakim Rubinstein released his decision not to prosecute: he was highly critical of aspects of Netanyahu's conduct, including the prolonged failure to pay a contractor's bills, but ruled that the investigation had not produced sufficient evidence for bribe-taking or other charges; he noted that about 100 gifts to the state were unaccounted for but lacked evidence to charge Netanyahu or his wife.
court: Israel Police; Attorney General of Israel
presumption_note: No charges were brought; the attorney general found insufficient evidence. Netanyahu is presumed innocent.
key_facts: 1999–2000: police recommend charges
27 September 2000: attorney general decides not to indict

case: Benjamin and Sara Netanyahu v. Igal Sarna (defamation)
description: Benjamin and Sara Netanyahu sued Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Igal Sarna over a Facebook post claiming that Sara Netanyahu had kicked her husband out of their car during a fight. Both testified in court in March 2017; Sarna said he had sources for the claim.
outcome: Judgment for the plaintiffs: on 11 June 2017 the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court ruled that the post was libellous and aimed at harming the couple's reputation, and ordered Sarna to pay more than $25,000 in damages to the couple. Netanyahu and his wife said ‘justice has been done’.
presumption_note: Civil proceeding in which Netanyahu was the plaintiff; it concerned no allegation against him.
key_facts: March 2017: Netanyahus testify
11 June 2017: court awards damages to the Netanyahus

description: Netanyahu, his wife Sara and son Yair sued former prime minister Ehud Olmert over an April 2021 interview in which Olmert said the three suffered from ‘mental illness’. Olmert argued in court that he had voiced an opinion, not a diagnosis.
outcome: Judgment for the plaintiffs: on 21 November 2022 Judge Amit Yariv of the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court ruled that Olmert had defamed the family, noting that ‘calling someone mentally ill can be humiliating for a person’, and ordered him to pay NIS 62,500 (about $18,000) in damages (AFP via L'Orient Today). Whether Olmert appealed was not established in the sources consulted.
presumption_note: Civil proceeding in which Netanyahu was a plaintiff; it concerned no allegation against him.
key_facts: April 2021: Olmert's remarks in a television interview
21 November 2022: court rules for the Netanyahus; NIS 62,500 in damages

case: Netanyahu v. Haaretz, Yedioth Ahronoth, Ynet, Channel 12 and six journalists (defamation, reports of pre-7 October warnings)
description: On 8 September 2026 Haaretz published an investigation by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, drawn from their book on the hostages, reporting, citing unnamed sources, that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed had spoken with Netanyahu by phone in late September 2023 and warned him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major ‘surprise’, and that Netanyahu did not pass the warning to the security chiefs. Netanyahu's office called the report a fabrication and said official records show no contact between the two from 1 September to 7 October 2023; the UAE first declined to comment, and an Emirati official later denied that bin Zayed had personally warned Netanyahu of an imminent attack, while Israeli media cited a New York Times report in which five Israeli officials supported the account. Haaretz refused Netanyahu's demand for a retraction, an apology and NIS 1 million, saying it would defend the reporting in court.
outcome: On 29 September 2026 Netanyahu filed suit in the Jerusalem District Court seeking at least NIS 2.6 million from Haaretz, Yedioth Ahronoth, Ynet and Channel 12 and from journalists Shlomi Eldar, Ruth Yuval, Uri Misgav, Nadav Eyal, Barak Ravid and Attila Somfalvi, also covering a Ynet report, based on The Wall Street Journal, that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had warned him in October 2023. The defendants have 60 days from service to file their defence. No hearing had been reported as of 22 October 2026.
presumption_note: Civil proceeding in which Netanyahu is the plaintiff. The underlying reports rely on unnamed sources and are disputed; Netanyahu denies receiving either warning, and no court has ruled on their accuracy.
key_facts: 8 September 2026: Haaretz report published
29 September 2026: suit filed seeking NIS 2.6 million
Defendants may plead truth and public interest or responsible journalism under Israeli defamation law
